name: Lepchajagat
tagline: A forest village on the Ghoom–Sukhia road, named for the Lepchas
meta_description: Lepchajagat near Darjeeling: Lepcha lore, dawn Kanchenjunga, forest and bird walks, the WBFDC resort, homestays from ₹1,500 pp and shared jeep fares.
summary: Lepchajagat is a small forest village at about 2,120 m, 19 km from Darjeeling on the road from Ghoom to Sukhia Pokhari. Conifer, oak and rhododendron forest, dawn views of Kanchenjunga, birding and afternoon mist are the draw. Stay at the six-room WBFDC resort or a village homestay for ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals.

local_story.title: The world of the Lepchas, in a forest of mist
paras: The name says whose land this was. Jagat means place, or world, and the Lepchas are the oldest people of these hills, living in the forests of Sikkim and Darjeeling long before Bhutia, Nepali or British arrivals. They call themselves Rongkup, often translated as children of the snowy peak. Lepcha elders tell that the first man and woman, Fudongthing and Nazongnyu, were made from the snows of Kanchenjunga, which the Lepchas honour as a guardian. In a village named for them, standing at dawn and facing that mountain is worth a quiet thought.

The road through Lepchajagat runs along the ridge from Ghoom toward Sukhia Pokhari, and on to Mirik and Maneybhanjan. Much of the land on either side is reserved forest, with tall conifers planted in British times alongside older stands of oak and rhododendron. That is why the village feels so different from the open tea slopes elsewhere in the district: thick trunks wrapped in moss and ferns, needles soft underfoot and cloud moving between the trees most afternoons. Houses sit in small clearings along the road, and the village has stayed small, with forest pressing in on both sides.

Tourism here grew around the forest. The West Bengal Forest Development Corporation runs a small nature resort of six rooms in the village, and families around it opened homestays as Lepchajagat became known as a quiet base near Darjeeling. It still has very few attractions in the usual sense. What you do is walk, watch birds, look at the mountain when it shows itself and sit in the cold with a cup of tea while the mist comes and goes. For many people that is the whole point.

did_you_know: At about 2,120 m, Lepchajagat sits slightly higher than Darjeeling town at around 2,042 m, so its nights are usually a little colder.

Lepcha tradition says the first man and woman, Fudongthing and Nazongnyu, were made from the snows of Kanchenjunga; the Lepchas call themselves Rongkup, often translated as 'children of the snowy peak'.
The WBFDC Nature & Wilderness Resort at Lepchajagat has only six rooms, two with balconies, and its online bookings open 90 days ahead, so peak dates go quickly.
intro: Lepchajagat is the closest real forest stay to Darjeeling. Nineteen kilometres from town, past Ghoom, the road enters tall conifer and oak forest, and a scatter of houses, a few homestays and the forest corporation's small resort appear in the clearings. There is no market, no mall and very little traffic after dark. Mornings can be sharp and clear, with Kanchenjunga lit up from the village viewpoint; by afternoon the mist usually rolls in through the trees and you see a few metres ahead. Both are the point.

Come for one or two nights between October and May. Use it as a quiet base for Darjeeling sights, a stop between Darjeeling and Mirik, or a rest from the crowds on Chowrasta. Shared jeeps between Darjeeling and Sukhia Pokhari or Mirik pass through, so it is easy and cheap to reach. Rooms are few, though, and the WBFDC resort books out early: plan ahead for October, December and the May–June holidays.

highlights.title: Dawn from the village viewpoint
highlights.text: A short walk from the road leads to open ground looking north over the ridges to Kanchenjunga. Arrive 20 minutes before sunrise between October and April; on clear days the massif turns from grey to pink to white in a few minutes, and you will share it with a handful of people at most.

highlights.title: Forest walks under the conifers
highlights.text: Forest roads and village paths lead off the main road into tall conifer, oak and rhododendron forest. Walk an hour in almost any direction for moss, ferns, birdsong and silence. Keep to clear paths, go in pairs and come back before the afternoon mist cuts visibility.

highlights.title: Birding at the forest edge
highlights.text: Early mornings bring mixed flocks along the forest edge: tits, yuhinas, laughingthrushes, minivets, sibias and, with luck, woodpeckers and barbets. March to May is the busiest season for song. Bring binoculars; there are no hides or marked trails, just the road and the edge of the trees.

highlights.title: Mist in the afternoon
highlights.text: Most afternoons, especially from April onwards, cloud climbs up from the valleys and fills the forest. Visibility drops to a few metres, the air turns damp and still, and the conifers become outlines. It is cold and very beautiful. Have tea indoors, or walk slowly along the road in a bright jacket.

highlights.title: A base between Darjeeling and Mirik
highlights.text: Lepchajagat sits on the road from Ghoom to Sukhia Pokhari, Mirik and Maneybhanjan. That makes it an easy stop between Darjeeling and Mirik, a quiet base for a day in town, or a night before the drive to the Sandakphu road head at Maneybhanjan.

highlights.title: Jorepokhri and Sukhia close by
highlights.text: The twin ponds of Jorepokhri and the market town of Sukhia Pokhari are a short drive on. Combine them in a half-day: walk around the ponds, have momos in Sukhia, and carry on to the Simana viewpoint on the Mirik road for a look into Nepal's Ilam hills.

how_to_reach.text: Jeeps for Sukhia Pokhari, Mirik and Maneybhanjan leave from Darjeeling's motor stand and pass through Ghoom and Lepchajagat. Ask to be dropped at Lepchajagat; seats cost about ₹60–100 and the ride takes 45 minutes to an hour. Coming back, wait by the road and wave down a jeep with space.
A car from Darjeeling costs ₹1,200–1,800 one way and takes about 45 minutes. From NJP or Bagdogra expect ₹3,500–4,500 and 3–3.5 hours, either via Ghoom or via Mirik and Sukhia Pokhari.

Shared jeeps between Mirik and Darjeeling run via Simana, Sukhia Pokhari and Lepchajagat; ask for the Lepchajagat stop. From Siliguri, a shared jeep to Mirik followed by a Darjeeling-bound jeep is the cheapest way in.

where_to_stay: The best-known stay is the WBFDC Nature & Wilderness Resort, run by the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation: six rooms, two with balconies, set in the forest. It is booked on the WBFDC online portal, which opens 90 days ahead; check current status before you travel. Around it, village families run homestays along the road and in the clearings, typically ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. There are not many rooms in total, so book ahead for October, December and the May–June holidays. If everything is full, stay in Ghoom or Darjeeling and come out early for the dawn and a forest walk.
tips: Book the WBFDC resort as soon as the 90-day window opens if your dates fall in October, December or May.
Pack a proper warm jacket, hat and gloves even in spring, because at 2,120 m nights are colder than in Darjeeling.
Walk in the forest in the morning and be back before the afternoon mist, which can cut visibility to a few metres.
Carry a torch, since the road is unlit and very dark at night and power cuts are common in storms.
Stock up on cash and snacks in Darjeeling or Ghoom, because the village has only a few small shops.

experiences.title: Kanchenjunga dawn from Lepchajagat
experiences.summary: A short walk in the dark to Lepchajagat's open viewpoint, a flask of tea and the first sun on Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m. A quiet alternative to the Tiger Hill crowd, 19 km from Darjeeling and a few minutes from your bed.
body: At 2,120 m, Lepchajagat sits above much of the surrounding country, and from open ground near the village the view runs north across ridge after ridge to the Kanchenjunga massif. At dawn on a clear day the summits catch the light first, turning pink, then gold, then white, while the valleys below are still dark and full of mist. Kanchenjunga, at 8,586 m the third-highest mountain on Earth, is the guardian of Lepcha tradition, which gives watching it from a village named for the Lepchas its own small weight.

Ask your host the evening before for the way and the walking time; from most stays it is only a few minutes. Aim to arrive 20 minutes before sunrise: about 5.10 am in October, 5.30 am in November and close to 6 am in December and January. It will be cold, often near freezing in mid-winter, so wear everything warm you have and take a flask. There is no fee, no tower and usually only a handful of people, many of them villagers out for a morning walk.

Clear mornings are most likely from October to early December and in March and April. From late April haze builds, and in the monsoon the peaks are hidden most days. If the first morning fails, try again the next; that is the argument for two nights. Afterwards, walk slowly back along the road as the birds start up at the forest edge and the village lights its kitchen fires. Breakfast will taste better for the cold.

faqs.q: Can we see Everest from Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: Not usually. Lepchajagat's view is of the Kanchenjunga massif to the north. Everest, Lhotse and Makalu show far to the west only from higher points such as Tiger Hill and Sandakphu, and only on very clear days. For a chance of Everest, add a Tiger Hill dawn from Darjeeling or Ghoom.

faqs.q: Is the Lepchajagat sunrise better than Tiger Hill?
faqs.a: It is quieter, not bigger. Tiger Hill, at about 2,567 m, is higher and has the wider panorama, but in season hundreds of people arrive by jeep before 5 am. Lepchajagat's viewpoint is free, close to your room and usually near-empty. For a calm sunrise, Lepchajagat is the better choice.

faqs.q: What should we wear for the dawn walk?
faqs.a: Layers: a thermal top, fleece, down or padded jacket, woolly hat, gloves and warm socks with good shoes. From December to February temperatures at dawn can be close to 0 °C. Carry a torch for the walk and a flask of tea, because you will stand still for half an hour.

experiences.title: Forest walk through conifer, oak and rhododendron
experiences.summary: A morning on foot through the forests around Lepchajagat: tall conifers, oak, rhododendron, moss and ferns, with the mist waiting for the afternoon. Easy walking on forest roads and village paths, best done before the cloud comes up.
body: Lepchajagat is wrapped in forest. Much of it is reserved forest, with tall conifers planted in rows in British times standing beside older mixed stands of oak and rhododendron. The trunks are thick with moss and ferns, and the ground is soft with needles. In March and April the rhododendrons flower red among the green, and after the monsoon the forest floor sprouts fungi in every colour. It is rare to find forest like this so close to a town the size of Darjeeling.

Ask your host to suggest a route; forest roads and village paths lead off in several directions, and villagers use them every day to collect firewood and fodder. A good plan is two to three hours: out along a forest road, a loop through a settlement and back for breakfast. Walking is easy, mostly level or gently rolling, but paths get muddy and slippery after rain. Do not leave the paths for dense forest, and do not walk alone; go in pairs or with someone from the village.

Start early. By noon the cloud usually climbs from the valleys, and within minutes the forest can turn into a grey room with five metres of visibility. That is a fine time to be on the road in a jacket and a bad time to be on an unknown path. Carry water, a rain jacket from April, and leech socks or salt in the monsoon. Take your litter back with you: there are few bins, and plastic lasts for decades in a forest.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk in the forest at Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: Yes, on established paths in daylight and in company. Wild animals are rarely seen and avoid people. The real risks are slippery ground, losing your way in mist and darkness falling early in winter. Tell your host where you are going, go in pairs and be back by mid-afternoon.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for the forest walk?
faqs.a: Not for simple walks along forest roads and village paths, which your host can explain. For longer routes or birding a local companion helps; ask your homestay whether someone can walk with you and agree a fee first, usually a few hundred rupees for a morning. There is no formal guide counter here.

faqs.q: When do the rhododendrons flower around Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: Mostly in March and April at this height, sometimes into early May. Flowering depends on the winter and on altitude, so trees lower down bloom a little before those on higher ridges. For whole hillsides of rhododendron in flower, the Singalila Ridge toward Sandakphu is the bigger show, in April and May.

experiences.title: Birding along the Lepchajagat forest edge
experiences.summary: An early morning with binoculars on the road and forest edge around Lepchajagat, where mixed flocks of Himalayan birds move through the trees. No hides and no fees; just patience, a field guide and a flask of tea.
body: The forests between Ghoom and Sukhia Pokhari lie at the height where many birds of the eastern Himalayan temperate forest live. On a good morning at Lepchajagat you might see flocks of tits and yuhinas working through the canopy, sibias calling from the treetops, laughingthrushes rummaging in the undergrowth and minivets flashing red and yellow. Woodpeckers drum on dead trunks, and barbets call loudly and repeatedly from somewhere you can never quite find. None of this is guaranteed. That is birding.

Start at first light, when birds are most active, and work slowly along the road and the forest edge, where light reaches the lower branches. Stand still near fruiting or flowering trees and let the flocks come to you. Spring, from March to May, brings the most song and colour as birds breed; October and November are clear and calm. In the monsoon birds are active, but rain and mist make watching hard. Bring binoculars, a field guide or a bird app, and patience.

There are no hides, no trail markers and no fees here, which is part of the charm and part of the challenge. Keep noise low, never use playback to call birds in the breeding season, and do not leave the road for dense forest alone. If you are serious about your list, combine Lepchajagat with Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary near Tiger Hill, declared in 1915 and one of the oldest sanctuaries in India, for a wider range of species in a few days.

faqs.q: What birds can we see at Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: Typical birds of forest at around 2,000 m: tits, yuhinas, sibias, laughingthrushes, minivets, woodpeckers, barbets and flycatchers, with thrushes and finches in winter. Sightings vary with season and luck. Spring mornings from March to May are usually the most rewarding, with birds singing and in breeding colour.

faqs.q: Is there a birding guide in Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: There is no formal guide service in the village. Some homestay families know the local birds well, and Darjeeling has birders who take people out for a fee. Ask your host first. If you hire anyone, agree the price and hours in advance, and say clearly which birds or habitats you hope for.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year for birding here?
faqs.a: March to May is best, when resident birds breed and sing. October and November are good too, with clear, calm mornings. Winter brings some birds down from higher ridges. June to September is wet and misty, which makes watching difficult even though the birds are still around.

experiences.title: Half-day to Sukhia Pokhari and Jorepokhri
experiences.summary: A half-day from Lepchajagat to the market town of Sukhia Pokhari, the twin ponds of Jorepokhri and the Simana viewpoint looking into Nepal. Cheap by shared jeep, easy by car, and a good use of a misty afternoon.
body: Lepchajagat is quiet by design, so when you want a change of scene, go a few kilometres along the road. Sukhia Pokhari is the local market town and junction: jeeps for Mirik, Maneybhanjan and Darjeeling meet here, and shops sell everything from vegetables to blankets. Jorepokhri, about 4 km beyond Sukhia, has the twin ponds that gave it its name and a sanctuary declared in 1985 for the Himalayan salamander. Simana, on the Mirik road, looks west across the border into the tea hills of Ilam in Nepal.

By shared jeep, flag one down on the road toward Sukhia, walk around the market and then take a local car to Jorepokhri. By car, a half-day from Lepchajagat including Simana costs ₹1,500–2,500. At Jorepokhri, walk the path around the two ponds and read the boards about the salamander, but do not expect to see one: 2026 reporting by Mongabay says paving and tourist works have changed the ponds so much that the newts no longer breed there.

Back in Sukhia, find a tea shop on the main road and order momos or aloo dum with tea, then watch the jeeps load and unload: schoolchildren, farmers with sacks, trekkers heading for Maneybhanjan and Sandakphu. It is ordinary hill life, and that is the attraction. Be back at Lepchajagat by mid-afternoon if you want a last walk before dark, or time it to arrive with the mist and spend the evening by the heater.

faqs.q: How far are Sukhia Pokhari and Jorepokhri from Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: Both are a short drive along the same road. Sukhia Pokhari is a few kilometres on from Lepchajagat, and Jorepokhri about 4 km beyond Sukhia. By car the whole loop with Simana takes four to five hours with stops, and shared jeeps cover the Lepchajagat to Sukhia stretch for a small fare.

faqs.q: Will we see salamanders at Jorepokhri?
faqs.a: Probably not, and we would rather say so. Jorepokhri was declared India's first salamander sanctuary in 1985, but 2026 reporting by Mongabay says concrete paving and tourist works have changed the ponds so much that salamanders no longer breed there. Go for the forest walk and the story, not a sighting.

faqs.q: Can we cross into Nepal from Simana?
faqs.a: Indian citizens usually walk across to Pashupati market at Pashupatinagar with valid photo ID, such as a voter ID or passport, and no visa. Foreign nationals generally cannot use this crossing. Rules and checks change, so carry ID for everyone in your group and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Lepchajagat from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 19 km, 45 minutes to an hour by road via Ghoom on the road to Sukhia Pokhari and Mirik. A shared jeep seat costs about ₹60–100 and a reserved car ₹1,200–1,800 one way. Jeeps bound for Sukhia, Mirik or Maneybhanjan pass through the village, so getting there is easy.

faqs.q: What does Lepchajagat mean?
faqs.a: It means the place, or world, of the Lepchas, jagat being place or world. The Lepchas are the oldest inhabitants of the Darjeeling and Sikkim hills, with their own language, script and traditions centred on Kanchenjunga. The village keeps their name, though the hills around are now home to people of many communities.

faqs.q: How do we book the WBFDC resort at Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: Online on the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation's booking portal, which opens 90 days before the stay date. The resort has six rooms, two with balconies, so October, December and May dates go quickly. Check current status and rates on the portal before you travel, and carry ID that matches the booking.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: October to early December for the clearest Kanchenjunga dawns, and March to May for rhododendrons and birdsong. December to February are very cold, roughly 0–8 °C, but often clear. June to September is wet and misty almost every day, with leeches in the forest, though some travellers love the mist.

faqs.q: Is Lepchajagat worth a night, or just a stop?
faqs.a: Stay a night if you like forest, quiet and early mornings. Most tours stop for 20 minutes on the way to Mirik, which shows you a viewpoint and a tea stall. The real Lepchajagat is the dawn, the forest walk before the mist and the silence after dark. One or two nights is right.

faqs.q: Is Lepchajagat good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes, for a calm night or two. The drive from Darjeeling is short, the walks are gentle, and children usually enjoy the forest and the mist. There is little else to do, so pair it with Darjeeling's zoo and the toy train. Pack plenty of warm clothes, because nights are colder than in town.

faqs.q: Does it snow in Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: Rarely. Light snow falls on the ridges around Darjeeling in some winters, usually in January or February, and Lepchajagat, at about 2,120 m, may get a dusting, but you cannot plan for it. For more reliable winter snow, look at Sandakphu, Tsomgo Lake or North Sikkim instead.

faqs.q: How much should we budget per day in Lepchajagat?
faqs.a: About ₹2,000–3,000 per person per day. Homestays run ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast, snacks and tea add ₹150–300, and shared jeeps cost under ₹100 a ride. A reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra, ₹3,500–4,500, is the biggest single cost; shared jeeps via Darjeeling or Mirik are far cheaper.

faqs.q: Can we visit Lepchajagat on a day trip from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes, easily. Shared jeeps take 45 minutes to an hour, or join a Mirik day tour, which usually stops here. Come early for a forest walk and lunch, and return before dark. But the dawn view and the mist-filled evenings are the reason to come, and those need an overnight stay.
